reader.title: Barnwell County night-rider intimidation (1880)
bases: A3 describes armed night riders who cursed, abused and threatened Black landowners and warned them off Republican meetings, with no killing or reported injury.
The night visits are reported only in Frederick Nix, Jr.'s partisan letter (A3); A1, A2, A4 and A6 concern the preceding Blackville meeting, not the riders.

summary.text: The Barnwell County night-rider intimidation of 1880 was a series of night visits by a band of armed riders to Black farmers in Barnwell County, South Carolina, in late July or early August 1880, warning them never again to attend a Republican meeting for Garfield.

It is known from a single letter by Frederick Nix, Jr., Republican chairman of the county, dated Blackville, August 11, which placed the visits within a wider campaign of retaliation against Black Republicans after a ratification meeting at Blackville on July 27.
No one was reported killed or hurt, no victims were named, and the letter reached print through the Philadelphia Press and a Pennsylvania weekly.
Barnwell County Republicans called a meeting at Blackville for Tuesday, July 27, 1880, to ratify the nominations of Garfield and Arthur, with E. W. M. Mackey and W. N. Taft advertised as speakers.

Beforehand the Barnwell People invited all Democratic candidates to attend, and the Barnwell Sentinel told Democratic clubs to send representatives "who will nail lies to the wall as fast as they are told."
A Charleston dispatch to the New York Times identified those clubs as the "Red Shirt, Rifle and Sabre Clubs" it blamed for the 1876 killings at Ellenton, a few miles from Blackville.
By Nix's account the meeting went ahead despite Democratic efforts to keep Black people away, with "between five and six thousand colored Republicans" present.
A Boston Herald comment later reprinted in Tallahassee likewise said the meeting "was not disturbed."

Nix wrote that the county commissioners had ordered men out to work the public roads for three days beginning July 28, but that the start was moved to July 26 once the meeting was announced, and only about twenty-five of four or five hundred men were told.

Men who reported on the 28th were turned away; hundreds, he said, were then arrested and fined $10 to $15 or jailed for fifteen to thirty days, while many sharecroppers were "discharged and driven from off the farms" where they worked.

Black men who farmed their own land were dealt with differently: they were visited by "a band of these armed midnight riders," who cursed, abused and threatened them and warned them never to attend another Garfield Republican meeting.
The letter gave no date, place or names for these visits, and did not say how many riders took part or how many farms they reached.
Nix described Black ministers traveling the county to raise money to free church members from jail, and others hiding "in the woods and swamps" to avoid arrest.
He said complaints reached him hourly from the county's Garfield and Arthur clubs, and closed that Black Republicans remained "determined to cast their votes for Garfield and Arthur."
No report of any arrest of the riders or official inquiry into the visits appears in the coverage.

The account first ran in the Philadelphia Press, and The Post of Middleburg, Pennsylvania, reprinted it on August 26 under the headline "South Carolina Bull-Dozing" and the subhead "How the Republicans of Barnwell County are Being Persecuted."

Its framing matched what Northern Republican papers had said of Blackville in advance: the Portland Daily Press, quoting Penn. Weekly Notes, wrote that the meeting would be "attended, i.e., broken up, by the Democrats," and the Boston Advertiser, reprinted in Wisconsin in September, concluded that South Carolina "can be carried for him only by violence."

The opposing line appeared in the Weekly Floridian, which reprinted the Boston Herald's argument that Republicans had predicted the Blackville meeting would be stopped and then "changed their tune" when it was not.
None of these papers mentioned the night riders, and no South Carolina paper or Black newspaper in the coverage reported the visits.

accounts.label: Republican county chairman's letter
accounts.gist: After the July 27 Blackville meeting, Black Republicans were punished through a manipulated road-work order, arrests and fines, evictions, and night visits by armed riders warning landowners never to attend another Garfield meeting.

accounts.label: Boston Herald (via Weekly Floridian)
accounts.gist: The Blackville meeting itself 'was not disturbed', contrary to Republican predictions; says nothing of later night visits.

framing.detail: The Post headlined the letter 'South Carolina Bull-Dozing' and 'How the Republicans of Barnwell County are Being Persecuted'; the letter calls the treatment 'unlawful' and 'gross, inhuman'.
Northern Republican papers anticipated violence at Blackville, reading Barnwell Democratic notices as a plan to break up the meeting.
The Weekly Floridian reprinted the Boston Herald's charge that Republicans had wrongly predicted the Blackville meeting would not be permitted.
